Sachertorte

Sachertorte is Vienna's most famous cake: a dense, lightly sweet dark chocolate sponge layered with apricot jam under a glossy dark chocolate glaze. Created in 1832 for a Viennese prince, it's traditionally served with a generous spoon of unsweetened whipped cream.

Cake Austria Sweet Hard

The Seven-Year Cake War

The recipe was invented in 1832 by 16-year-old apprentice Franz Sacher for Prince Metternich. Decades later the Hotel Sacher and the Demel bakery fought a seven-year court battle over who could call their cake the "Original Sacher-Torte" — and whether the jam belongs in the middle of the cake or only under the glaze. The hotel won.

The Recipe

Yield 12–14 slices
Prep Time 40 minutes
Baking Time 45–55 minutes
Total Time 4 hours

What you'll need

  • 23cm (9 inch) springform pan
  • Stand mixer or hand mixer
  • Mixing bowls
  • Fine sieve
  • Rubber spatula
  • Long serrated knife
  • Offset spatula
  • Wire rack set over a tray (to catch glaze)
  • Instant-read thermometer

Ingredients

Cake

  • 170g (6 oz) dark chocolate (50–55%), chopped
  • 170g (¾ cup) unsalted butter, softened
  • 110g (1 cup) confectioners' (icing) sugar
  • 6 large eggs, separated, room temperature
  • 1 tsp vanilla extract
  • 135g (⅔ cup) granulated sugar
  • 130g (1 cup) all-purpose flour
  • Pinch of salt

Apricot filling

  • 240g (¾ cup) apricot jam
  • 1 tbsp rum (or water)

Chocolate glaze

  • 200g (1 cup) granulated sugar
  • 80ml (⅓ cup) water
  • 115g (4 oz) dark chocolate (50–55%), finely chopped

To serve

  • 250ml (1 cup) heavy cream, whipped to soft peaks, unsweetened

Instructions

  1. Prep the pan and oven Preheat the oven to 180°C (350°F). Butter a 23cm springform pan, line the base with parchment, and lightly flour the sides.
  2. Melt the chocolate Melt the 170g chopped chocolate gently — over a pan of barely simmering water or in short microwave bursts — then set aside to cool until just warm.
  3. Cream the butter base Beat the softened butter with the confectioners' sugar until pale and fluffy, about 3 minutes. Beat in the vanilla and the cooled melted chocolate, then add the egg yolks one at a time, beating well after each.
  4. Whip the whites In a clean bowl, whip the egg whites with the pinch of salt to soft peaks. Add the granulated sugar a spoonful at a time, whipping to stiff, glossy peaks.
  5. Fold together Stir about a third of the whites into the chocolate base to loosen it. Gently fold in the remaining whites in two additions, alternating with the sifted flour, until just combined — don't knock out the air.
  6. Bake Spread the batter evenly in the pan. Bake for 45–55 minutes, until a skewer inserted in the center comes out clean. The top will dome and crack slightly — that's normal. Cool in the pan for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a rack, peel off the parchment, and cool completely (about 1½ hours).
  7. Fill with apricot Warm the apricot jam with the rum until fluid, then press through a sieve. Slice the cooled cake horizontally into two even layers with a serrated knife. Brush the cut side of the bottom layer with jam, replace the top, then brush a thin coat of jam over the entire cake, top and sides. Let it set for 15 minutes.
  8. Make the glaze Combine the sugar and water in a small saucepan and bring to a boil. Boil, without stirring, until it reaches 108°C (226°F) on a thermometer, about 5 minutes. Remove from the heat, add the finely chopped chocolate, and stir until completely smooth. Let cool, stirring occasionally, until it thickens to a pourable coating consistency — around 32°C (90°F).
  9. Glaze and set Set the cake on a rack over a tray. Pour all the glaze onto the center in one go and quickly spread it over the top and down the sides with an offset spatula, working fast before it sets — minimal passes give the smoothest finish. Leave to set at room temperature (not the fridge, which dulls the shine), at least 1 hour.
  10. Serve Slice with a warm, dry knife and serve each piece with a spoon of unsweetened whipped cream on the side.

Tips & Notes

  • Sachertorte is famously dry by design — the apricot jam and the whipped cream are what carry the moisture, so don't skip either
  • It's better the next day: once glazed, keep it under a cake dome at room temperature and serve within 3–4 days
  • For a more forgiving glaze, skip the sugar syrup and pour over a warm ganache instead (150g dark chocolate melted into 150ml hot cream) — softer and less mirror-like, but nearly foolproof
  • Use a chocolate you'd happily eat on its own; at 50–55% it stays true to the classic, which is less bitter than most modern chocolate cakes
